title: 2 Chronicles 24:1–16
context: Joash, preserved as an infant from Athaliah's purge and crowned through the priest Jehoiada (chapters 22–23), begins a forty-year reign. He does right all the days of Jehoiada. He resolves to restore the LORD's house, presses the slow Levites, and has a chest set at the temple gate for the tax Moses laid on Israel. The people give gladly, the house is repaired, and vessels are made from the remainder. Jehoiada dies at a great age and is buried among the kings. This parallels 2 Kings 12:1–16, which differs in several details.

verses.text: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah, of Beersheba.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash is seven at his accession and reigns forty years; his mother is Zibiah of Beersheba. Arminian readers note that a child king depends heavily on those who guide him, which gives his counselors great influence and responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse parallels 2 Kings 12:1. The young king's survival through Athaliah's purge (2 Kings 11:2) shows God preserving the line of David when it hung by a single child.

verses.text: Joash did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash does right "all the days of Jehoiada the priest." Arminian readers note, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 12:2, that the phrase signals his faithfulness was tied to Jehoiada's influence and would change after his death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:2 reads "all his days in which Jehoiada the priest instructed him." The Chronicler's wording points ahead to the decline that follows the priest's death in verses 17–22.

verses.text: Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he became the father of sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiada takes two wives for Joash, and he has sons and daughters. Arminian readers note that the detail shows Jehoiada's continuing guardianship, securing the future of David's line after it had nearly been destroyed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this detail is not in 2 Kings 12. Children for Joash mean the survival of David's house, which Athaliah had tried to wipe out; the narrator records the arrangement without comment on its form.

verses.text: After this, Joash intended to restore the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash intends to restore the LORD's house. Arminian readers note the king's own initiative and zeal for God's house during the years he walked under Jehoiada's influence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the temple, damaged under Athaliah, becomes the focus of Joash's best work. Concern for God's house is a recurring mark of the faithful kings in Chronicles.

verses.text: He gathered together the priests and the Levites, and said to them, “Go out to the cities of Judah, and gather money to repair the house of your God from all Israel from year to year. See that you expedite this matter.” However the Levites didn’t do it right away.
verses.arminianNotes: Joash sends priests and Levites to gather money yearly, "however the Levites didn't do it right away." Arminian readers note that even good plans can stall when those responsible delay.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:6 dates the delay to Joash's twenty-third year and speaks of the priests. The Chronicler names the Levites; the difference is noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: The king called for Jehoiada the chief, and said to him, “Why haven’t you required of the Levites to bring in the tax of Moses the servant of the LORD, and of the assembly of Israel, out of Judah and out of Jerusalem, for the Tent of the Testimony?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks Jehoiada why the Levites have not collected "the tax of Moses." Arminian readers note the king holding even the chief priest accountable for neglected duty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler grounds the collection in the law of Moses for "the Tent of the Testimony." The repair is presented as obedience to God's word, not a royal innovation.

verses.text: For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken up God’s house; and they also gave all the dedicated things of the LORD’s house to the Baals.
verses.arminianNotes: Athaliah's sons had broken up God's house and given its dedicated things to the Baals. Arminian readers see the damage done by a ruler's free choice to promote false worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler explains the need for repair by naming the desecration under Athaliah, "that wicked woman." Restoration answers years of deliberate apostasy.

verses.text: So the king commanded, and they made a chest, and set it outside at the gate of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: A chest is made and set "outside at the gate of the LORD's house." Arminian readers note the practical solution that let the people give directly toward the work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:9 says Jehoiada set the chest "beside the altar" with a hole in its lid. The placement is described differently in the two accounts, and the difference is left standing.

verses.text: They made a proclamation through Judah and Jerusalem, to bring in for the LORD the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: A proclamation calls Judah and Jerusalem to bring the tax Moses laid on Israel. Arminian readers note that the people are invited to respond, giving them a share in restoring God's house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the repeated reference to Moses. The Chronicler presents the collection as a return to the pattern God gave in the wilderness for the support of his sanctuary.

verses.text: All the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had filled it.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes and people rejoice and fill the chest. Arminian readers see glad, willing giving, the kind of free response God delights in when his people are called to support his work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that joyful giving is a frequent theme in Chronicles. When God's people are rightly led, they give gladly for the sake of his house.

verses.text: Whenever the chest was brought to the king’s officers by the hand of the Levites, and when they saw that there was much money, the king’s scribe and the chief priest’s officer came and emptied the chest, and took it, and carried it to its place again. Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance.
verses.arminianNotes: The chest is emptied day by day by the king's scribe and the chief priest's officer, and money is gathered in abundance. Arminian readers note the careful accountability built into the process.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the joint oversight of royal and priestly officers protected the integrity of the offerings. Faithful handling of money given to God is part of honoring him.

verses.text: The king and Jehoiada gave it to those who did the work of the service of the LORD’s house. They hired masons and carpenters to restore the LORD’s house, and also those who worked iron and bronze to repair the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: The king and Jehoiada hire masons, carpenters, and workers in iron and bronze. Arminian readers note that the gifts of the people are put directly to work through skilled laborers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the work required many hands and skills. God's house is restored through ordinary craftsmen whose labor serves his worship.

verses.text: So the workmen worked, and the work of repairing went forward in their hands. They set up God’s house as it was designed, and strengthened it.
verses.arminianNotes: The work goes forward, and they set up God's house "as it was designed." Arminian readers see a faithful completion of the task, the result of willing giving and diligent work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase "as it was designed." The restoration returns the house to its intended pattern rather than reshaping it to new preferences.

verses.text: When they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, from which were made vessels for the LORD’s house, even vessels with which to minister and to offer, including spoons and vessels of gold and silver. They offered burnt offerings in the LORD’s house continually all the days of Jehoiada.
verses.arminianNotes: From the remaining money, vessels of gold and silver are made, and offerings continue "all the days of Jehoiada." Arminian readers note that 2 Kings 12:13 says vessels were not made from the money brought in; the accounts differ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the difference with 2 Kings 12:13 and leave it standing here. The verse's closing phrase again ties Judah's worship to Jehoiada's lifetime, preparing for what follows his death.

verses.text: But Jehoiada grew old and was full of days, and he died. He was one hundred thirty years old when he died.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiada dies "full of days" at one hundred thirty. Arminian readers note the long life of a faithful servant whose influence held Joash and Judah on a right course.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that "full of days" is language used of patriarchs. The Chronicler honors Jehoiada's long faithfulness, though his death will expose how much depended on him.

verses.text: They buried him in David’s city among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Jehoiada is buried in David's city among the kings, "because he had done good in Israel." Arminian readers see public honor given to a faithful life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the remarkable honor of a priest buried among kings. The contrast with Joash, who will not be buried in the tombs of the kings (24:25), is pointed.
